F1.quote: Machine-Mediated Reception Studies · EA-MMRS-TINP-01 · working notebook v0.24 · deposited 16 November 2026 · supersedes v0.21 (#1772)
F1.claim: the paper: Lee Sharks, This Is Not Philosophy, MMRS, working notebook v0.24, deposited 16 November 2026, superseding #1772

F2.quote: the author's correspondence with Ronald Polansky, editor of Ancient Philosophy (Duquesne), 23 July – 9 September 2026. Four threads and 41 messages, read in full with quoted replies stripped
F2.claim: the correspondence read: four threads, 41 messages, 23 July – 9 September 2026, with the editor of Ancient Philosophy (Duquesne)

F3.quote: The author's ruling (15 November): the correspondence is with the editor in his official capacity, on the substance of his field. It is institutional, not private, and it is quoted as such.
F3.claim: the ruling: the correspondence is institutional and quoted as such

F4.quote: Scope, ruled the same day: his responses to the submissions and near-submissions, and what he looks for in submissions, are quoted. His statements of his own views are not.
F4.claim: the scope of quotation: responses to submissions and what the editor looks for, never his own views

F5.quote: In Ancient Philosophy, 8 of 844 articles open the question of what the object is; across the sister journals since 2021, 4 of 283 Plato/Aristotle abstracts do.
F5.claim: the headline count: 8 of 844 articles; 4 of 283 abstracts in the sister journals since 2021

F6.quote: the ancient field repairs a named object, the continental field pairs names, the analytic field takes a position in a debate, and the form of the abstract converges on the analytic
F6.claim: three placements of one unit across the fields

F7.quote: In the Archiv für Geschichte der Philosophie of the 1890s one ancient title in five puts a work's standing in question, and its pages carry the question at that rate until the war; by the 1920s it is gone.
F7.claim: the Archiv baseline: one ancient title in five in the 1890s; gone by the 1920s

F8.quote: The notebook argues that disciplinarity is the stable form of the article economy: the journal certifies the person through a unit that cannot fail, and the field takes the shape of what can be certified.
F8.claim: the thesis: disciplinarity as the stable form of the article economy

F9.quote: In three approaches to the journal, carrying three states of its evidence, the condition of admission was the same, the claim withdrawn.
F9.claim: three approaches, one condition of admission

F10.quote: submitted to Ancient Philosophy in July 2026 and declined on 28 August
F10.claim: Socrates as Orthonym submitted in July 2026, declined 28 August

F11.quote: Socrates as Orthonym, submitted; revised 24 July; tightened 3 August (37 pages, abstract 97 words)
F11.claim: the first approach: submitted, revised 24 July, tightened 3 August

F12.quote: The earnable condition is stated once, as results (0B.5), and the version written to meet it was not the version read.
F12.claim: the version written to meet the stated condition was not the version read

F13.claim: the third approach (9 September): a query letter with no manuscript

F14.quote: "If the paper is not about Aristotle and Theophrastus being one person, but instead that the two works mentioned are closely connected, this could be O.K." (9 September). "Could we see a tamer version of this paper" (2 September).
F14.claim: the editor's condition on the query (9 September) and his request of 2 September, quoted under the ruling as responses to submissions

F15.quote: The November framework (#1754) records how the programme developed; it was not before the editor in August or September, and nothing here treats it as if it were.
F15.claim: the November framework was not before the editor

F16.quote: The editor of a specialist journal, Ronald Polansky of Ancient Philosophy, without referees he could find for an unusual submission, read the paper himself. He corresponded at length and gave practical advice: length, clarity, abstract, a narrower object, the state of the secondary literature. When the manuscript did not meet the journal's standards, he declined it, and he left the door open for a different paper.
F16.claim: the conventional reading of the exchange, stated first and in full

F17.quote: On this reading nothing in the exchange is a mechanism. It is an editor doing his job with more patience than most.

F18.quote: An extraordinary claim needs extraordinary evidence, and an editor who declines to spend referees on it exercises the judgment the post exists for.
F18.claim: the conventional reading of the case

F19.quote: "I frequently request that authors rid papers of philosophical jargon" (23 July)
F19.claim: what the editor asks of submissions: vocabulary
F19.lineage: what the editor asks of submissions

F20.quote: "My recommendation... is instead to do some close analysis of an ancient text rather than such broad stroke sort of writing" (28 August)
F20.claim: what the editor asks of submissions: close analysis of an ancient text
F20.lineage: what the editor asks of submissions

F21.quote: "It should begin with a discussion of the present state of thinking about the relationship of the two works, i.e., coverage of available secondary discussion" (9 September)
F21.claim: what the editor asks of submissions: the secondary discussion first
F21.lineage: what the editor asks of submissions

F22.claim: what the editor asks of submissions: length
F22.lineage: what the editor asks of submissions

F23.quote: Of Socrates as Orthonym: "We seem able to arrive at the same results without the hypothesis" (28 August)
F23.claim: the editor's response to Socrates as Orthonym

F24.quote: The decline of 28 August lists among its grounds a prior version on Academia ("whether there should be multiple publications of versions of a paper") and "whether papers composed by A.I. participation should be considered as regular submissions".
F24.claim: the grounds of the decline of 28 August include a prior version online and AI participation

F25.quote: The demands are the specification of the field's unit, stated by the person who administers it.
F25.claim: the archive's reading: the demands as the specification of the unit
F25.lineage: the archive's reading of the exchange

F26.quote: The demands are reasonable in form and close the route in effect, the same split the CRJ audit found between procedural check and substantive judgment.
F26.claim: reasonable in form, closing the route in effect
F26.lineage: the archive's reading of the exchange

F27.quote: "We seem able to arrive at the same results without the hypothesis" is the one demand the author took as the real review (28 August): a hypothesis must earn a result the received partition strains for.
F27.claim: the objection kept as the real review
F27.lineage: the archive's reading of the exchange

F28.quote: Three exchanges cannot by themselves show what every development of the evidence would meet. The claim does not rest on them. It follows from the structure of the question, and the letters are its instance.
F28.claim: the limit: three exchanges; the claim rests on the structure of the question
F28.lineage: the archive's reading of the exchange

F29.quote: (1) An admitted case, in any field, of independently attested persons merged into one maker on textual evidence alone; none was found here, and the search is open.
F29.lineage: the archive's reading of the exchange

F30.quote: the largest object the field opens is the individual work, and the partition of a corpus into persons is a different kind of object
F30.claim: the difference of type between the work and the partition

F31.quote: The field widened for thirty years, from 1980 to 2019. Then it narrowed sharply after 2020, back to the Plato+Aristotle share of the early 1980s.
F31.claim: the topic range of the journal: widening 1980–2019, narrowing after 2020

F32.quote: Articles on the Platonic Letters: 0. … On the unwritten doctrines: 1. … On Theophrastus: 1.
F32.claim: the tails: Letters 0, unwritten doctrines 1, Theophrastus 1

F33.quote: Read by hand, 8 of 844 ask what the text is. Three put a work's standing in question: the Lysis's authenticity (1990), the dating of the anonymous Parmenides commentary (2000), and the authorship of Philoponus on De anima iii (2022). Five concern text and fragments
F33.claim: the eight: three on a work's standing, five on text and fragments

F34.quote: 94 readable abstracts, 2022–26, read and coded one by one by the lead coder.

F35.quote: A, a passage re-read: 29%. … B, an inconsistency resolved: 27%, rising from 21% (2022–23) to 30% (2024–26). … C, a doctrine reconstructed inside one author: 32%. … D, a claim about the text itself: 3%. All three D cases confirm the object whole: the Axiochus, the unity of the Phaedrus, and the Divisiones Aristoteleae.
F35.claim: the reach codes in the journal, 2022–26

F36.quote: In Ancient Philosophy, it holds. B is 27% there and rising, against 13–17% in the sisters as adjudicated; only Apeiron approaches it (24% in 2021–26).
F36.claim: the prediction holds in the journal

F37.quote: The narrowing belongs to the field, not to one journal. Ancient Philosophy comes to it late and sharply.
F37.claim: the narrowing is the field's; the journal comes to it late and sharply

F38.quote: That is agreement within the Claude coding procedure, the readers' consistency with the lead instance's classifications; it is not independent validation of those classifications, which would need a human second coder.
F38.claim: the coding's limit: agreement within the Claude procedure; no human second coder

F39.quote: Titles are not arguments. Regex coding misreads (see 4.3). An abstract is not the article.
F39.claim: the census's limits: titles, regex, abstracts

F40.quote: The editor of Ancient Philosophy, declining a submission (28 August 2026), lists "whether papers composed by A.I. participation should be considered as regular submissions" among the grounds
F40.claim: the ancient gate on AI, as #1773's table gives it

F41.quote: The ancient gate is one editor on one submission. The test to strengthen it is the census journals' own author guidelines and decline practice, read journal by journal.
F41.claim: the gate comparison's limit, and the test it names

F42.quote: In the ancient sets the work stays inside one author (A+B+C) in 87%, against the field's 71–76%
F42.claim: the model test: the model's ancient abstracts stay inside one author more than the field's

F43.quote: Not one generated abstract asks what a text is: no authenticity, no date, no unity, no edition.
F43.claim: the model test: no claim about the text in sixty ancient abstracts

F44.quote: The CRJ audit (#1770) is the first field; Ancient Philosophy is the second.
F44.claim: the combined audit: the journal is its second station

F45.quote: The census holds articles that examine a single work's standing (§4.8); it holds none that examines the partition.
F45.claim: the census holds no article examining the partition

F46.quote: Ancient Philosophy Today: DIALOGOI is a peer-reviewed journal of ancient philosophy published by Edinburgh University Press, whose first issue appeared in April 2019.
F46.claim: Dialogoi: a different journal, Edinburgh University Press, first issue April 2019
